analysis.one_liner: Lets people hit hard by COVID-19 wipe out student loan debt in bankruptcy.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing or a vote: it sat in the House Judiciary Committee from July 2020 until the Congress ended in January 2021.
analysis.plain_summary: Normally, student loan debt is nearly impossible to erase in bankruptcy — you must prove 'undue hardship,' a bar almost no one clears. This bill would have punched a narrow exception into that rule for the pandemic: a borrower whose pre-tax income fell by 20% to 40% (the required drop rising with income, and only for people earning under $200,000 threshold tiers) during the COVID-19 outbreak, or whose family's primary earner died or was seriously disabled by COVID-19, could have wiped out their student loans through bankruptcy. It also applied the same relief to loans made or guaranteed by the government and private lenders alike.
analysis.who_benefits: Borrowers whose income collapsed during the pandemic — lower-income borrowers faced the lowest bar (a 20% income drop if they earned under $75,000) — and families that lost a primary earner to COVID-19. This is a group of people who, under existing law, generally cannot discharge student loans no matter how desperate their situation becomes.

how_it_helps.text: A borrower whose pre-tax income fell at least 20% (if they previously earned under $75,000), 30% (under $125,000), or 40% (above that) during the COVID-19 outbreak could discharge student loans in bankruptcy.
If the primary income earner of a borrower's family died or became seriously disabled from COVID-19, the borrower could also discharge student loans in bankruptcy.
The relief window covered income declines starting January 21, 2020 and lasting until 60 days after the COVID-19 emergency ended.

analysis.who_pays: Student loan lenders and debt collectors — including the federal government as the holder of most student debt — would eat the losses on loans wiped out in bankruptcy, spreading the cost to taxpayers. That cost is the price of relief for borrowers who would otherwise be stuck with debt through no fault of their own.
analysis.who_pays_short: Student loan holders and debt collectors

drawbacks.text: The bill gave no relief to borrowers whose hardship showed up other ways — for example, someone who lost a job and took a lower-paying one after the measured window, or whose income decline predated the January 2020 starting point, would not qualify.
Bankruptcy itself carries lasting credit damage and legal costs, so the relief comes through a process that is expensive and stigmatizing rather than direct forgiveness.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The relief is well-targeted — it keys to demonstrated income collapse or a COVID death or disability in the family, with the bankruptcy bar dropping steeply for lower earners — but it is narrow. It does nothing for borrowers distressed in other ways, and it channels relief through the bankruptcy system, which is slow and costly for the debtor. Still, for the borrowers it reaches, it removes a barrier that currently makes student debt effectively permanent.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Judiciary Committee the day it was introduced, and the committee never held a hearing, markup, or vote on it before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Mary Gay Scanlon introduced the bill on July 16, 2020, with five Democratic cosponsors including Judiciary Committee Chairman Jerrold Nadler.

The House referred it to the Committee on the Judiciary the same day, and no further action — no hearing, no markup, no floor vote — appears in its history before the 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Student loan lenders, collectors, and the federal loan portfolio are better off because the bill died: the current near-impossible 'undue hardship' standard stays in place, and pandemic-distressed borrowers keep paying.

for.name: Rep. Mary Gay Scanlon
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to create a COVID-specific bankruptcy discharge for student loans.

for.name: Rep. Jerrold Nadler
for.role: Chairman, House Judiciary Committee; original cosponsor
for.what_they_did: Signed on as an original cosponsor of the bill, which was referred to his own committee.

against.name: House Committee on the Judiciary
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on July 16, 2020 and never scheduled a hearing, markup, or vote on it for the rest of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: All six supporters — the sponsor and five cosponsors — were Democrats, and no Republican cosponsored or acted on the bill; it died in committee without a recorded vote.

industries.industry: Student loan lenders and debt collectors
industries.note: The bill would let qualifying borrowers erase student debt in bankruptcy, converting currently bulletproof loans into collectible-only-until-discharge ones. These interests benefit from the status quo, in which student loans survive bankruptcy in almost every case.

industries.industry: Federal government (as holder of most student debt)
industries.note: Most student loans are federal, so discharges would write down the government's loan portfolio — a real fiscal cost that is the direct counterpart of relief for distressed borrowers.
